subject: settings for parallel analysis on a cluster

messages.author: 95e9261d3e867527
messages.subject: settings for parallel analysis on a cluster
parts:
Hi Nick / All,

I was wondering if anybody has experience running BioGeoBEARS on a cluster using the parallel analysis settings. I have a large dataset that will not finish in time if I don't run it in parallel. However, I've been having trouble getting the settings right. I know it varies from cluster to cluster, but it would be helpful if anybody has an example of their set-up that works. I am using a multi-threaded job (all CPUs on the same compute node).

My job settings for the cluster look something like this:

#$ -S /bin/sh
#$ -pe mthread 4
#$ -q sThC.q
#$ -l mres=32G,h_data=8G,h_vmem=8G,himem

In my BioGeoBEARS run, I set

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$num_cores_to_use = 4
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$cluster_already_open = parallel::makeCluster(4, type = "FORK")
(other settings below)

This works for a small dataset (17 spp, 3 areas total, with max. 3 areas), but when I scale it up a little (25 spp, 6 areas total, max areas per sp 3), it just hangs until it runs out of memory and dies. The second dataset finishes in under 15 min or so when run in non-parallel mode on my laptop. I've also tried snow::makeCluster(4, type = "MPI") but I get some scary error messages about "Open MPI is currently operating in a condition that could result in memory corruption or other system errors".

Thanks!

Here are the rest of the settings:

# Intitialize a default model (DEC model)
  BioGeoBEARS_run_object = BioGeoBEARS::define_BioGeoBEARS_run()
 
  # Give BioGeoBEARS the location of the phylogeny Newick file
# (I define the paths elsewhere)
  BioGeoBEARS_run_object$trfn = trfn
 
  # Give BioGeoBEARS the location of the geography text file
  BioGeoBEARS_run_object$geogfn = geogfn
 
  # Input the maximum range size
  BioGeoBEARS_run_object$max_range_size = 3
 
  BioGeoBEARS_run_object$min_branchlength =  0.000001    # Min to treat tip as a direct ancestor (no speciation event)
  BioGeoBEARS_run_object$include_null_range = TRUE    # set to FALSE for e.g. DEC* model, DEC*+J, etc.
 
  # Speed options and multicore processing if desired
  BioGeoBEARS_run_object$on_NaN_error = -1e50    # returns very low lnL if parameters produce NaN error (underflow check)
  BioGeoBEARS_run_object$speedup = TRUE          # shorcuts to speed ML search; use FALSE if worried (e.g. >3 params)
  BioGeoBEARS_run_object$use_optimx = "GenSA"    # if FALSE, use optim() instead of optimx()
  BioGeoBEARS_run_object$num_cores_to_use = 4
  BioGeoBEARS_run_object$cluster_already_open = parallel::makeCluster(4, type = "FORK")
 
  BioGeoBEARS_run_object$force_sparse = FALSE    # force_sparse=TRUE causes pathology & isn't much faster at this scale
 
  # This function loads the dispersal multiplier matrix etc. from the text files into the model object. Required for these to work!
  # (It also runs some checks on these inputs for certain errors.)
  BioGeoBEARS_run_object = BioGeoBEARS::readfiles_BioGeoBEARS_run(BioGeoBEARS_run_object)
 
  # Good default settings to get ancestral states
  BioGeoBEARS_run_object$return_condlikes_table = TRUE
  BioGeoBEARS_run_object$calc_TTL_loglike_from_condlikes_table = TRUE
  BioGeoBEARS_run_object$calc_ancprobs = TRUE    # get ancestral states from optim run

messages.author: 115d05260b0c341a
messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] settings for parallel analysis on a cluster
parts:
Hi Joel,

Back at ANU I had a try with getting multicore stuff in R to run on their cluster, and I failed completely, even after many back-and-forths with the tech support.

I think the key is this: if you can, inside R, type the command

detectCores()

...and it says you have 20 cores (or whatever) available, then BioGeoBEARS can easily run on those 20 cores (or however many you set "num_cores_to_use" to), using normal methods.

If not, then you are stuck trying to figure out some totally different method of multicore processing with R, probably requiring a re-write of the multicore-using functions in BioGeoBEARS.

Cheers!
Nick

PS: A separate issue is that a sufficiently large state space will still allocate a matrix so huge (10,000 x 10,000 or whatever) that the memory fills up and your job/computer hangs/crashes.  Multicores won't help with this, you have to be able to hold the matrix and run each matrix exponentiation on a single core, the parallelization is just doing the matrix exponentiations for separate branches on separate cores.

parts:
Hi Nick,

Thanks so much for the response!

I had neglected to post the output that showed up before it crashed:

```
Your computer has 72 cores.

Your computer has 72 cores. You have chosen to use:
num_cores_to_use = 4 cores for the matrix exponentiations in the likelihood calculations.
Cluster with 4 cores already open.

NOTE: You are optimizing with GenSA::GenSA() ('Generalized Simulated Annealing') instead of optimx() or optim(). GenSA seems to be better for more complex problems (4+ parameters, wildly different scalings). However, it will likely be slower, as it does more calculations of the likelihood to search the parameter space.

NOTE: Before running GenSA::GenSA(), here is a test calculation of the data likelihood
using calc_loglike_for_optim() on initial parameter values, with printlevel=2...
if this crashes, the error messages are more helpful
than those from inside GenSA::GenSA().
```

It looks from your code that the "Your computer has 72 cores" part is coming from detectCores() anyways right? So according to that, it should work.

The part that confuses me is that this test dataset is quite small: 42 states according to numstates_from_numareas(numareas=6, maxareas=3, include_null_range=TRUE), and 25 taxa. Like I said it finishes quickly on my laptop not running in parallel. So all I can deduce so far is that the jobs are hanging somewhere and just sucking memory until they hit the limit set by the cluster settings.

And the even more confusing part is that as I mentioned originally, it does finish fine in parallel with an even smaller dataset.

Is this the line in the code where the matrix exponentiations get split up?

https://github.com/nmatzke/BioGeoBEARS/blob/c32ca4f50985f6407ff7f0ad368cf24539e05643/R/calc_loglike_sp_v01.R#L3121

If that's the only part that needs to be changed I may be able to do it with a different package.

Thanks for explaining about the limits of parallelization! So it sounds like parallelization can help if you have a gigantic tree, but not if you just have too many range states to begin with, correct?

Best,

Joel

> Hi Nick,
>
> Thanks so much for the response!
>
> I had neglected to post the output that showed up before it crashed:
>
> ```
> Your computer has 72 cores.
>
> Your computer has 72 cores. You have chosen to use:
> num_cores_to_use = 4 cores for the matrix exponentiations in the
> likelihood calculations.
> Cluster with 4 cores already open.
>
> NOTE: You are optimizing with GenSA::GenSA() ('Generalized Simulated
> Annealing') instead of optimx() or optim(). GenSA seems to be better for
> more complex problems (4+ parameters, wildly different scalings). However,
> it will likely be slower, as it does more calculations of the likelihood to
> search the parameter space.
>
> NOTE: Before running GenSA::GenSA(), here is a test calculation of the
> data likelihood
> using calc_loglike_for_optim() on initial parameter values, with
> printlevel=2...
> if this crashes, the error messages are more helpful
> than those from inside GenSA::GenSA().
> ```
>
> It looks from your code that the "Your computer has 72 cores" part is
> coming from detectCores() anyways right? So according to that, it should
> work.
>
Yes...

>
> The part that confuses me is that this test dataset is quite small: 42
> states according to numstates_from_numareas(numareas=6, maxareas=3,
> include_null_range=TRUE), and 25 taxa. Like I said it finishes quickly on
> my laptop not running in parallel. So all I can deduce so far is that the
> jobs are hanging somewhere and just sucking memory until they hit the limit
> set by the cluster settings.
>
> And the even more confusing part is that as I mentioned originally, it
> does finish fine in parallel with an even smaller dataset.
>

Yeah, that sounds like some fundamental issue with the job-passer stuff on
the cluster.  You could check it with some simple test code using e.g.
mapply(), mcmapply(), clusterApply(), etc., and see if those work.

You may also have to check if you need library(snow) or library(parallel),
these have some complex history and some of those functions ended up in R
base.

>
> Is this the line in the code where the matrix exponentiations get split up?
>
>
> https://github.com/nmatzke/BioGeoBEARS/blob/c32ca4f50985f6407ff7f0ad368cf24539e05643/R/calc_loglike_sp_v01.R#L3121
>
> If that's the only part that needs to be changed I may be able to do it
> with a different package.
>
Yep!

>
> Thanks for explaining about the limits of parallelization! So it sounds
> like parallelization can help if you have a gigantic tree, but not if you
> just have too many range states to begin with, correct?
>

Yes!  Although, if you have, say, a 2500x2500 matrix, you would definitely
want to parallelize even on a small tree, a tree with 20 branches could run
~20 times faster.

Cheers!
Nick

>
> Best,
>
> Joel
>
> On Wednesday, March 25, 2020 at 5:56:56 PM UTC+9, Nick Matzke wrote:
>>
>> Hi Joel,
>>
>> Back at ANU I had a try with getting multicore stuff in R to run on their
>> cluster, and I failed completely, even after many back-and-forths with the
>> tech support.
>>
>> I think the key is this: if you can, inside R, type the command
>>
>> detectCores()
>>
>> ...and it says you have 20 cores (or whatever) available,
>> then BioGeoBEARS can easily run on those 20 cores (or however many you set
>> "num_cores_to_use" to), using normal methods.
>>
>> If not, then you are stuck trying to figure out some totally different
>> method of multicore processing with R, probably requiring a re-write of the
>> multicore-using functions in BioGeoBEARS.
>>
>> Cheers!
>> Nick
>>
>> PS: A separate issue is that a sufficiently large state space will still
>> allocate a matrix so huge (10,000 x 10,000 or whatever) that the memory
>> fills up and your job/computer hangs/crashes.  Multicores won't help with
>> this, you have to be able to hold t

messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] settings for parallel analysis on a cluster
parts:
Hi Nick,

I've been doing some more debugging and realized I have a completely different problem to what I think it was originally.

It doesn't have to do with running things in parallel (although I'm very glad for the information you gave me about that!)

It comes down to some difference between the setup on the cluster and on my laptop.

I tried running the exact same data (1 core only) on my laptop and on the cluster, and it works on my laptop but fails on the cluster. The thing that really gets me is that I'm using a docker image, so everything *should* be exactly the same. However I'm using it through udocker (https://github.com/indigo-dc/udocker) on the cluster since they don't allow standard docker. So maybe there's some subtle difference there.

Anyways, I've tracked it down to expokit_dgpadm_Qmat2(), which is apparently just calling rexpokit::expokit_dgpadm_Qmat(). It doesn't issue an error, but instead just hangs without ever finishing. Do you have any ideas about why that function might differ between a cluster and a laptop? Are there some external dependencies that might vary? I'm kind of grasping at straws here, but please let me know if you have any ideas...

Best,

Joel

messages.author: 115d05260b0c341a
messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] settings for parallel analysis on a cluster
parts:
Hi -- well, that does get you closer. expokit_dgpadm_Qmat() is the core function calling matrix exponentiation code from the FORTRAN library EXPOKIT. This code is compiled in the R package rexpokit. If you were able to do compile-from-source for rexpokit on the cluster, it might work better than whatever image was uploaded.  A pure "hang" like that suggests a memory leak or something, but rexpokit has been through a bunch of rounds of R CMD check over the years to meet CRAN's checkers there. So it may just be that whatever rexpokit image you have on your udocker doesn't work on the cluster.

Unfortunately I don't have much more help than that, but give compiling a try!

Cheers,
Nick
